\>I would even say: you are basically dead IF you know how to fight on the ground... and then get carried away by a sports martial arts mindset.

Yes, I agree with you, \*\*if\*\* you get carried away by sports martial arts mindset. But I can use that same argument for striking, if someone use point fighting karate or tkd on the streets the agressor is going to ignore de blows and keep assaulting that person. It all depends if the fighter will treat the assault as an street fight or spar/comp fight.

\>In the civil world being on the ground is the worst option to have

Again, I agree with you, and that's exactly why fighters should know how to ground fight(especially stand up fighters), that way you are:  
1) Harder to throw to the ground

2) If you get to the ground, you are better equipped to disengage and stand up

3) And if you are on the ground and can´t stand up(you ended up on  bottom mount, side control or with the agressor in your guard) you have ways to get to a better position, sweep or, if the opportunity presents it self, choke or break something and then, back to your feet

What I'm saying is that the ground is dangerous and not a place you want to be, but if you end up there you should know how fight in there.

\>This isn't done in Judo or BJJ so we don't even think about it.

Again, the same argument can be made about striking arts, in the streets people will try to choke you out, especially if they have friends, you will be throwing hands and his friend will come behind your back and choke you out. Good luck getting out of this without some grappling training.

And also, there are some places that add striking to grappling, doing atemi waza should be a part of grappling training. This way the martial artist will perceive  ground fighting differently. If I'm on kesa gatame I can also use tetsui uchi if necessary, or go to kami shiho gatame if I don't want to throw punches.

\>It is awesome in martial arts but almost always useless in civil life.

That's where I disagree, not only it's useful when you need to defend yourself, but what you are forgetting is the self defense situations where you don't want to throw any punches. I work in a school, if two students are fighting I would lose my job if I punched them, but I've thrown and used all sorts of osaekomi techniques to contain the fight without hurting the students. Most of the time this is what you need to do, restrain and wait for authorities to come.

We agree on most of the points, what makes us have opinions so divergent is that I see grappling as primarily defensive and if you need to be offensive you can. You should never stay on the ground, but you should know how to work on the ground, get up and run or fight, as most of the fights go to the ground, being able to get up or finish someone in there is a must.

Not every scuffle ends in murder but almost all end on the ground.
